content.text: Overall Design Synopsis
This is a Phase 3, randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, parallel-group, multicenter, global superiority study.

Population: Adults with previously untreated Stage IIIB/IIIC NSCLC not amenable to curative therapy, or Stage IV NSCLC; PD-L1 tumor proportion score (TPS) ≥1% by central testing; no actionable genomic alterations; Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status 0 or 1; and measurable disease. Key exclusions are untreated brain metastases, active autoimmune disease, prior pneumonitis, anti-angiogenic class-related bleeding or thrombotic risk, and unstable liver disease or uncontrolled hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection (Section 5.1).

Assignment: Randomization 1:1 by interactive response technology (IRT) after eligibility is confirmed within the 28-day screening period, stratified by PD-L1 TPS (1% to 49% vs ≥50%) and histology (squamous vs nonsquamous).

Blinding and oversight: Double-blind; an unblinded pharmacist prepares masked infusions of identical duration. An independent data monitoring committee (IDMC) reviews unblinded safety data and the interim analysis of OS.
This study design includes participant, caregiver, investigator, and assessor masking.
Brief Summary

The purpose of this study is to measure how long participants live without their cancer getting worse with Drug A intravenous (IV) infusion compared with Drug B IV infusion in participants with advanced non-small cell lung cancer that has not been treated before. Participants will be assigned by chance to Drug A or Drug B, and neither participants nor study doctors will know which medicine is given. Study details include:
The study duration will be up to approximately 48 months.
The treatment duration will be up to 24 months (35 treatment cycles).
The visit frequency will be every 3 weeks during treatment and every 12 weeks during follow-up.
Number of Participants

Approximately 1000 participants will be screened to achieve 600 randomized (300 per arm). The primary PFS analysis will occur after approximately 331 events (90% power for HR 0.70; 2-sided α 0.05), and the final OS analysis after approximately 380 deaths (80% power for HR 0.75).
Study Arms and Duration
Arm A: Drug A 20 mg/kg IV Q3W. Arm B: Drug B 200 mg IV Q3W. Both are given for up to 35 cycles (approximately 24 months) or until BICR-confirmed progression, unacceptable toxicity, or withdrawal.
Periods: Screening up to 28 days; treatment; safety follow-up 30 days after the last dose; tumor imaging until progression; survival follow-up every 12 weeks.
Dose modification: No dose reductions; dose delays up to 12 weeks; discontinuation rules for immune-mediated, anti-angiogenic class, and liver events (Sections 6.4 and 7.1).
Data Monitoring/Other Committee
Yes
An IDMC, a BICR, a Safety Review Board, and a Steering Committee will support the study (Section 11.4).

This Phase 3 study will determine whether Drug A is superior to Drug B, an approved immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI), as first-line treatment for adults with locally advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) whose tumors express programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1). Drug A is a novel, humanized, bispecific immunoglobulin G1 (IgG1) antibody that combines immune checkpoint inhibition with anti-angiogenic activity.

This trial addresses the need for improved first-line treatment for adults with PD-L1-positive advanced NSCLC without actionable genomic alterations. The trial rationale and supporting background are presented in Sections 2.1.1 and 2.1.2, respectively.

Drug B monotherapy is a standard first-line treatment for PD-L1-positive advanced NSCLC without actionable genomic alterations, but most patients experience disease progression within the first year. In the Phase 2 study Demo-00201, Drug A produced a median progression-free survival (PFS) of 10.2 months with a manageable safety profile, compared with approximately 6 months expected with ICI monotherapy in a similar population. This study will determine whether Drug A is superior to Drug B in prolonging PFS.

A detailed description of the chemistry, pharmacology, efficacy, and safety of Drug A is provided in the Investigator's Brochure (IB). Information on Drug B is provided in the locally approved prescribing information.

content.text: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide, and NSCLC accounts for approximately 85% of cases. For patients without actionable genomic alterations, first-line options include ICI monotherapy for tumors expressing PD-L1, or immunotherapy combined with platinum-based chemotherapy (Hendriks 2023). Drug B monotherapy is approved for patients with PD-L1 tumor proportion score (TPS) ≥1% and improved overall survival (OS) compared with chemotherapy in this population. Drug B monotherapy is frequently selected for patients who prefer to avoid chemotherapy-related toxicity; however, median PFS with ICI monotherapy remains under 1 year, and most patients ultimately progress.

content.text: Drug B is the standard against which new first-line treatments for this population are judged, so a randomized superiority comparison with Drug B provides the most direct evidence of clinical benefit. Drug A shares immune checkpoint inhibition with Drug B and adds anti-angiogenic activity, which counteracts tumor immunosuppression; any improvement over Drug B can therefore be attributed to the additional activity of Drug A. Randomized evidence that adding anti-angiogenic therapy to immune checkpoint inhibition improves outcomes in NSCLC (Socinski 2018), together with the Phase 2 results for Drug A (Section 2.1.2), supports the assumed PFS hazard ratio of 0.70 (Section 10.11).

content.text: In nonclinical studies, binding of the angiogenic ligand increased the avidity of Drug A for its checkpoint target by more than 15-fold, and Drug A produced greater tumor growth inhibition in syngeneic models than an ICI alone. An Fc-silencing modification minimizes antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and cytokine release. In the Phase 1 study Demo-00101 (N=78; 3 to 30 mg/kg every 3 weeks [Q3W]), no maximum tolerated dose was reached, and doses ≥10 mg/kg maintained >95% peripheral checkpoint receptor occupancy and complete suppression of the free angiogenic ligand at trough. In the Phase 2 study Demo-00201, 120 participants with previously untreated PD-L1-positive NSCLC received Drug A 20 mg/kg Q3W. The confirmed objective response rate (ORR) was 48% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 39% to 57%), and median PFS was 10.2 months. The terminal half-life of Drug A is approximately 7 days, and steady state is reached by Cycle 4 (Investigator’s Brochure, Section 5.1).

content.text: Participants randomized to Drug A may experience improved disease control compared with standard ICI monotherapy, based on the antitumor activity observed in Study Demo-00201. Participants randomized to Drug B will receive an approved, guideline-recommended first-line treatment. All participants will receive close monitoring, including regular tumor imaging, laboratory tests, and physician assessments, which may permit earlier detection and management of disease progression and adverse events. Participation will also contribute to the development of a potential new treatment option for patients with NSCLC.

Taking into account the measures taken to minimize risk to participants participating in this study, the potential risks identified in association with Drug A are justified by the anticipated benefits that may be afforded to participants with previously untreated, PD-L1-positive, locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC.

content.text: This is a Phase 3, randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, parallel-group, multicenter, global superiority study of Drug A compared with Drug B as first-line treatment for PD-L1-positive, locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC. Approximately 600 participants will be randomized at approximately 250 sites in North America, Europe, and the Asia-Pacific region (Figure 1).

After a screening period of up to 28 days, eligible participants will be randomized 1:1 to Drug A 20 mg/kg IV Q3W or Drug B 200 mg IV Q3W, stratified by PD-L1 TPS (1% to 49% vs ≥50%) and histology (squamous vs nonsquamous).

Study intervention will continue until disease progression per RECIST v1.1 by BICR, unacceptable toxicity, withdrawal of consent, or a maximum of 35 cycles (approximately 24 months). Treatment beyond progression is permitted under the conditions in Section 7.1. Crossover between arms is not permitted.
Participants, caregivers, investigators, site staff, BICR reviewers, and the sponsor study team will be blinded to intervention assignment (Section 6.7.3).

After the last dose, participants will have a safety follow-up visit 30 days later, will continue tumor imaging until progression if they stopped treatment for another reason, and will be followed for survival every 12 weeks.
An independent data monitoring committee (IDMC) will review unblinded safety data approximately every 6 months and the interim analysis of OS (Section 10.9, Section 11.4).
This study design includes participant, caregiver, investigator, and assessor masking.

A patient advisory board of 8 people living with lung cancer and 2 caregivers reviewed the draft design. Based on their input, the visit schedule was aligned with treatment visits to minimize additional travel, patient-reported outcome (PRO) questionnaires were limited to 2 validated instruments, and telephone contact was permitted for survival follow-up. Participants will also have the option to complete a voluntary Study Participant Feedback Questionnaire on their clinical study experience.

A randomized, double-blind, active-controlled design provides an unbiased comparison of Drug A with a guideline-recommended standard of care. Blinding is feasible because both interventions are administered intravenously on the same schedule, and it reduces bias in investigator decisions on progression, treatment continuation, and AE attribution. A maximum treatment duration of 35 cycles is consistent with the approved duration of Drug B monotherapy and applies to both arms to avoid differential exposure.

Drug B monotherapy is approved and recommended by international guidelines as first-line treatment for PD-L1-positive (TPS ≥1%) advanced NSCLC without actionable genomic alterations (Hendriks 2023). A superiority comparison with Drug B therefore tests whether Drug A provides clinical benefit beyond the current ICI standard of care.

content.text: The interim analysis of OS provides an opportunity to establish an OS benefit before the final OS analysis, subject to the hierarchical testing procedure (see Section 10.10). 6.2.title: Rationale for Investigational Trial Intervention Dose and Regimen

content.text: The rationale for selection of the dose and regimen for each investigational trial intervention is presented in the Drug A and Drug B subsections below.

The Drug A dose of 20 mg/kg IV Q3W was selected on the basis of Phase 1 and Phase 2 data. Doses ≥10 mg/kg maintained >95% peripheral checkpoint receptor occupancy and complete suppression of the free angiogenic ligand throughout the dosing interval. Population PK modeling predicts that 20 mg/kg maintains trough concentrations above the target saturation concentration in >95% of patients, including those with high tumor burden or low serum albumin. Exposure-response analyses showed no increase in Grade ≥3 AEs between 10 and 30 mg/kg, and ORR was numerically higher at 20 mg/kg than at 10 mg/kg (48% vs 36%) (Investigator’s Brochure, Section 5.5).
Drug B will be administered at the approved dose of 200 mg IV Q3W for up to 35 cycles, consistent with the locally approved prescribing information.

Participants will receive Drug A 20 mg/kg or Drug B 200 mg by IV infusion on Day 1 of each 21-day cycle for up to 35 cycles (approximately 24 months), with masked infusions of identical duration prepared by an unblinded pharmacist. Retreatment criteria following a dose delay are provided in Section 6.3.1.
After a dose delay, the participant must meet all of the following criteria to be eligible for retreatment:
AE resolved to Grade ≤1 or baseline (Grade ≤2 for endocrinopathies controlled with replacement therapy).
Corticosteroid dose reduced to ≤10 mg/day prednisone equivalent.
Blood pressure controlled (<150/100 mmHg) and urine protein <2 g/24 hours, where applicable.
No ongoing study intervention discontinuation criterion (Section 7.1).

Dose reductions of Drug A or Drug B are not permitted. Toxicity will be managed by dose delay, infusion interruption, or permanent discontinuation according to Sections 6.4 to 6.4 and Section 12. Because the arm is blinded, the same rules apply to both arms. If both an immune-mediated and an anti-angiogenic class cause are possible, the more conservative action will be taken. Liver events will also be assessed against the liver event stopping criteria (Section 7.1.1.1).

Immune-mediated AEs will be managed according to the guidelines in Section 12, which are aligned with the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) and European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) recommendations (Schneider 2021; Brahmer 2021). In general, study intervention will be withheld for Grade 2 or 3 events and permanently discontinued for Grade 4 events, recurrent Grade 3 events, Grade 2 or higher pneumonitis that recurs, Grade 3 or higher myocarditis, or any event requiring more than 12 weeks to resolve. Systemic corticosteroids (prednisone 1 to 2 mg/kg/day or equivalent) will be started for Grade 2 or higher events and tapered over at least 4 weeks.

content.text: AE Definition
An AE is any untoward medical occurrence in a clinical study participant, temporally associated with the use of study intervention, whether or not considered related to the study intervention.

NOTE: An AE can therefore be any unfavorable and unintended sign (including an abnormal laboratory finding), symptom, or disease (new or exacerbated) temporally associated with the use of study intervention.
Events Meeting the AE Definition

Any abnormal laboratory test results (hematology, clinical chemistry, or urinalysis) or other safety assessments (eg, ECG, radiological scans, vital signs measurements), including those that worsen from baseline, considered clinically significant in the medical and scientific judgment of the investigator (ie, not related to progression of underlying disease, or more severe than expected for the participant’s condition)
Exacerbation of a chronic or intermittent pre-existing condition including either an increase in frequency and/or intensity of the condition
New condition detected or diagnosed after study intervention administration even though it may have been present before the start of the study.
Signs, symptoms, or the clinical sequelae of a suspected drug-drug interaction

Signs, symptoms, or the clinical sequelae of a suspected overdose of either study intervention or a concomitant medication. Overdose per se will not be reported as an AE/SAE unless it is an intentional overdose taken with possible suicidal/self-harming intent. Such overdoses should be reported regardless of sequelae.

Lack of efficacy or failure of expected pharmacological action per se will not be reported as an AE or SAE. Such instances will be captured in the efficacy assessments. However, the signs, symptoms, and/or clinical sequelae resulting from lack of efficacy will be reported as AE or SAE if they fulfill the definition of an AE or SAE.
Events not Meeting the AE Definition

Any abnormal laboratory findings or other abnormal safety assessments that are associated with the underlying disease, unless judged by the investigator to be more severe than expected for the participant’s condition.
The disease/disorder being studied or expected progression, signs, or symptoms of the disease/disorder being studied, unless more severe than expected for the participant’s condition.
Medical or surgical procedure (eg, endoscopy, appendectomy): the condition that leads to the procedure is the AE.
Situations in which an untoward medical occurrence did not occur (social and/or convenience admission to a hospital).
Anticipated day-to-day fluctuations of pre-existing disease(s) or condition(s) present or detected at the start of the study that do not worsen.
An SAE is defined as any untoward medical occurrence that, at any dose, meets one or more of the criteria listed:
a. Results in death
a. Is life threatening

The term life threatening in the definition of serious refers to an event in which the participant was at risk of death at the time of the event. It does not refer to an event, which hypothetically might have caused death, if it were more severe.
b. Requires inpatient hospitalization or prolongation of existing hospitalization

In general, hospitalization signifies that the participant has been admitted (usually involving at least an overnight stay) at the hospital or emergency ward for observation and/or treatment that would not have been appropriate in the physician’s office or outpatient setting. Complications that occur during hospitalization are AEs. If a complication prolongs hospitalization or fulfills any other serious criteria, the event is serious. When in doubt as to whether hospitalization occurred or was necessary, the AE should be considered serious.
Hospitalization for elective treatment of a pre-existing condition that did not worsen from baseline is not considered an AE.
c. Results in persistent or significant disability/incapacity
The term disability means a substantial disruption of a person’s ability to conduct normal life functions.

This definition is not intended to include experiences of relatively minor medical significance such as uncomplicated headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, influenza, and accidental trauma (eg, sprained ankle) that may interfere with or prevent everyday life functions but do not constitute a substantial disruption.
d. Is a congenital anomaly/birth defect
e. Is a suspected transmission of any infectious agent via an authorized medicinal product
f. Other situations:

Medical or scientific judgment should be exercised by the investigator in deciding whether SAE reporting is appropriate in other situations such as important medical events that that may not be immediately life-threatening or result in death or hospitalization but may jeopardize the participant or may require medical or surgical intervention to prevent one of the other outcomes listed in the above definition. These events should usually be considered serious.

Examples of such events include invasive or malignant cancers, intensive treatment in an emergency room or at home for allergic bronchospasm, blood dyscrasias, convulsions not resulting in hospitalization, or development of intervention dependency or intervention abuse.

This section is a summary of the planned statistical analyses of the most important estimands including primary and key secondary estimands.
General Considerations

All hypothesis tests will be 2-sided at an overall significance level of 0.05 (equivalent to 1-sided 0.025), and 95% CIs will be presented. Stratified analyses will use the stratification factors recorded in the IRT. If a stratum contains fewer than 5% of participants, strata will be pooled as specified in the SAP. Time-to-event endpoints will be summarized by Kaplan-Meier methods, with medians and 95% CIs (Brookmeyer-Crowley). 10.6.title: Analyses Associated with the Exploratory Objective(s)

content.text: Exploratory biomarker, exposure-response, and medical resource utilization analyses will be described in the SAP or separate analysis plans and reported separately from the clinical study report if needed.

Safety analyses will be performed in the SAS by actual intervention received. AEs will be coded using the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) and graded per NCI-CTCAE v5.0. Treatment-emergent AEs, SAEs, AESIs, immune-mediated AEs, AEs leading to interruption or discontinuation, and deaths will be summarized by arm. Laboratory shifts by worst post-baseline grade, liver chemistry elevations (including evaluation of drug-induced serious hepatotoxicity plots), vital signs, and exposure will be summarized descriptively.
Other analyses are described in Sections 10.8.1 and 10.8.2.
Population PK and exposure-response analyses of Drug A will be described in a separate analysis plan and reported separately.

PFS and OS HRs with 95% CIs will be presented in forest plots for prespecified subgroups, including PD-L1 TPS (1% to 49% vs ≥50%), histology, region, age (<65 vs ≥65 years), sex, ECOG performance status, smoking status, presence of brain or liver metastases, and ADA status (Drug A arm). Subgroup analyses are descriptive.

No interim analysis of PFS is planned. An interim analysis of OS will be performed by the IDMC, consisting of 3 clinicians and 1 statistician who are independent experts not otherwise involved in the study, at the time of the primary PFS analysis, when approximately 170 deaths (45% information fraction) are expected. Based on the group sequential design with the O’Brien-Fleming alpha spending approach (Lan-DeMets), a 1-sided alpha of 0.0008 (boundary HR ≈0.62) will be allocated to the interim analysis, and the final analysis at approximately 380 deaths will use a 1-sided alpha of 0.0247 (boundary HR ≈0.82). The boundaries will be recalculated from the observed number of deaths. No futility stopping rule is planned.

The interim analysis will be conducted such that the ongoing study integrity is maintained. Only the independent statistical support group, who is responsible for providing the interim analysis results to the IDMC will be unblinded to the individual treatment group assignments. Interim analysis results will not be shared with investigators, participants, or the study team who are involved in the conduct of the study before the final database lock.
The statistical analysis plan will describe the planned interim analyses in greater detail.

The type I error of α = 5% will be controlled in the strong sense using a hierarchical (fixed sequence) testing procedure. This is based on priority ordering of the null hypotheses and testing them in this order using the 2-sided 95% confidence interval approach until an insignificant result appears. Consequently, the second null hypothesis will only be tested if the first null hypothesis has been rejected in favor of Drug A. Operationally the hypotheses will be evaluated by 2-sided tests.

The testing order is PFS by BICR, then OS, then ORR by BICR. OS will be tested at the interim and final analyses using a Lan-DeMets alpha-spending function with O’Brien-Fleming boundaries (Section 10.9). ORR will be tested once, at the primary PFS analysis, only if both PFS and OS (at the interim or final analysis) are statistically significant; if OS becomes significant only at the final analysis, ORR will be tested at that time using the data from the primary PFS analysis.
Approximately 600 participants will be randomized. The sample size calculation is based on the primary efficacy estimand and its endpoint PFS by BICR.

It is assumed that median PFS is 6.0 months with Drug B and 8.6 months with Drug A (HR 0.70). Using the Schoenfeld method for a stratified log-rank test at a 2-sided significance level of 0.05, 331 PFS events provide 90% power. For OS, assuming median OS of 16.5 months with Drug B and an HR of 0.75, 380 deaths provide 80% power at a 2-sided significance level of 0.05, accounting for the interim analysis. Assuming uniform enrollment over 20 months and an annual dropout rate of 5%, the PFS analysis is expected approximately 20 months, and the final OS analysis approximately 41 months, after the first participant is randomized. Approximately 1000 participants are expected to be screened, assuming a screen failure rate of 40% (mainly because of PD-L1 status).

content.text: Restart refers to resuming the study intervention following liver stopping events for which there was a clear underlying cause (other than DILI) of the liver event (e.g., biliary obstruction, pancreatic events, hypotension, acute viral hepatitis). Furthermore, restart is not permitted following liver stopping event when the underlying cause was alcohol-related hepatitis (typically, alcohol-related hepatitis has AST>ALT and neither higher than 10xULN, in the context of reported or suspected heavy alcohol intake).

v10_sources.found_heading: Liver Safety: Study Intervention Restart/Rechallenge Guidelines

content.text: Rechallenge refers to resuming study intervention following study intervention induced liver injury (DILI). Following drug-induced liver injury, drug rechallenge is associated with a 13% mortality across all drugs in prospective studies. Clinical outcomes vary by drug, with nearly 50% fatality with halothane re-administered within one month of initial injury. However, some drugs seldom result in recurrent liver injury or fatality. Because of the risks associated with rechallenge after DILI, this should only be considered for a participant for whom there is compelling evidence of benefit from a critical or life-saving medicine, there is no alternative approved medicine available, and a benefit:risk assessment of rechallenge is considered to be favorable.
